{{Short description|Argumentation for the sake of winning the argument instead of reaching or seeking truth}}
{{Rhetoric}}
In [[philosophy]] and [[rhetoric]], '''eristic''' (from ''[[Eris (mythology)|Eris]]'', the ancient Greek [[goddess]] of chaos, strife, and discord) refers to an [[argument]] that aims to successfully dispute another's argument, rather than searching for [[truth]]. According to [[Terence Irwin|T.H. Irwin]], "It is characteristic of the eristic to think of some arguments as a way of defeating the other side, by showing that an opponent must assent to the negation of what he initially took himself to believe."<ref>Irwin, T.H. "Plato's Objection to the Sophists." The Greek World. London: Routledge, 1995. P. 585. Print.</ref> Eristic is defined by Rankin as arguing for the sake of conflict, as opposed to resolving conflict.<ref>H.D. Rankin (1983). Sophists, Socratics and Cynics. Pp. 233–237.</ref>

==Use in education==
Eristic was a type of "question-and-answer"<ref>Nehamas A., 1990, "Eristic, Antilogic, Sophistic, Dialectic: Plato's Demarcation of Philosophy from Sophistry", History of philosophy quarterly, Vol.7 (1) p.3-16 (page 6)</ref> teaching method popularized by the [[Sophism|Sophists]], such as [[Euthydemus of Chios|Euthydemos]] and [[Dionysodorus (sophist)|Dionysiodoros]]. Students learned eristic arguments to "refute their opponent, no matter whether he [said] yes or no in answer to their initial question".<ref>Irwin, T.H. "Plato's Objection to the Sophists." The Greek World. London: Routledge, 1995. 583. Print.</ref>
 
[[Plato]] contrasted this type of argument with [[dialectic]] and other more [[reason]]able and [[logic]]al methods (e.g., at [[The Republic (Plato)|''Republic'']] 454a). In the dialogue [[Euthydemus (dialogue)|''Euthydemus'']], Plato satirizes eristic. It is more than persuasion, and it is more than discourse. It is a combination that wins an argument without regard to truth. Plato believed that the eristic style "did not constitute a method of argument" because to argue eristically is to consciously use fallacious arguments, which therefore weakens one's position.<ref>Alexander Nehamas. "Eristic, Antilogic, Sophistic, Dialectic: Plato's Demarcation of Philosophy from Sophistry". (page 7).</ref>

Unlike Plato, [[Isocrates]] (often considered a Sophist) did not distinguish eristic from dialectic.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0168:book=5:section=454a|title=Plato, Republic, Book 5, section 454a|website=www.perseus.tufts.edu}}</ref> He held that both lacked a "'useful application' ... that created responsible citizens",<ref>Marsh, Charles. Classical rhetoric and modern public relations: an Isocratean model. New York: Routledge, 2013. P. 121.</ref> which unscrupulous teachers used for "enriching themselves at the expense of the youth."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0144:speech=15:section=45|title=Isocrates, Antidosis, section 45|website=www.perseus.tufts.edu}}</ref>

==Philosophical eristic==
[[Schopenhauer]] considers that only logic pursues truth. For him, [[dialectic]], [[sophistry]], and eristic have no objective truth in view, but only the appearance of it; he believed that they do not seek truth itself but, rather, victory. He names these three last methods as "eristic dialectic (contentious argument)."<ref>[http://coolhaus.de/art-of-controversy/eristii.htm Controversial Dialectic] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070715170819/http://coolhaus.de/art-of-controversy/eristii.htm |date=2007-07-15 }} on CoolHaus.de accessed at January 19, 2008</ref>

According to [[Schopenhauer]], [[The Art of Being Right|''Eristic Dialectic'']] is mainly concerned to tabulate and analyze dishonest stratagems,<ref>In his ''Dialectica Eristica'' Schopenhauer presents 38 eristic stratagems</ref> so that they may at once be recognized and defeated, in order to continue with a productive dialectic debate. It is for this very reason that Eristic Dialectic must admittedly take victory, and not objective truth, for its selfish aim and purpose.

==Argumentation theory==
[[Argumentation theory]] is a field of study that asks critical questions about eristic arguments and the other types of dialogue.
